acclimate

AK-luh-mayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To acclimate is to become accustomed to a new climate, environment, or situation.

Astronauts spend weeks in a special facility learning to acclimate to the disorienting effects of weightlessness before launch.

Example

Deep-sea divers must acclimate slowly to increasing water pressure, or risk serious injury on the way back up.

Acclimate is about the gradual process of adjusting to a new physical or situational condition.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

adapt: To adapt is to change your habits, gear, or methods so they work under new conditions -- the change is in what you do. To acclimate is different: you change nothing on purpose; your body and routine slowly grow comfortable with the new environment on their own.

adjust: To adjust is to make small changes so something fits new circumstances -- you adjust a strap, a mirror, a schedule in seconds. To acclimate is slower and larger: over days or weeks, your whole body or routine settles into a new climate or situation.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

resist: to refuse to accept or adjust to something new

reject: to refuse to accept something

Where it sits · how deep the adjustment goes — get used to → acclimate → assimilate

get used to vs. acclimate: Get used to is milder and shallower than acclimate -- you get used to a new alarm sound in a day or two, while acclimating means your whole body or routine slowly settles into a new environment.

assimilate vs. acclimate: Assimilate means to fully absorb into a new culture or environment, an even deeper adjustment than simply acclimating.

The pieces

prefix — ac-

prefix — ac-: to, toward (Latin ad-)

root — climate

root — climate: climate (Greek klima, 'region, zone')

Put it together

Put it together: Acclimate comes from ac- ('to, toward') + climate -- literally 'to adjust toward a climate.'
